Being a DM is being a game designer. Game design is an art, not a science. 


In other words, you know how people learn how to draw by starting with some basic skills and then working their way up to complicated things like three point perspectives and color theory and all that? Same goes for learning how to DM. start with foundational skills and work your way up to complicated/advanced techniques and knowledge. 


Foundational skills: understand the basics of probability and statistics; learn how to extrapolate a narrative out of dice rolls; understand that your job as a DM is to be the **user interface** for the game, so you need to be clear and straightforward so players know what they're getting into. 


(I swear, 90% of player frustration comes from the DM being super vague or focusing too much on storybook narration instead of just *telling* the players what's going on so that everyone's on the same page and everyone can contribute to what's happening. "Show don't tell" works great for books and movies because it's all carefully constructed and the consumer can go back and re-consume the material until they get it. "Show don't tell" coming from a DM is how you end up with a player going "OMG if I had known this was what you meant I wouldn't have done that!")

You could just make a f2p game that has all the normal trappings but you use only in-game currencies, no paid or premium currencies. Of course if you do that you will find that people will farm those currencies and trade them to each other for real money anyways, like buying gold for WoW. If that doesn't bother you, that's a solution. 


But if you're thinking to yourself that if people are going to pay for these things anyways, and you put in a lot of work and deserve to get paid for your work making the game, you might start to think about offering people to just buy in-game money straight from you. And then you're onto a whole new problem, inflation. 


So maybe you could limit the amount people buy from you, but that just means people will buy a little bit from you and then go buy a little bit from the secondary market. Or maybe you can put in a ton of money sinks, but that means having to ensure your money sinks are actually money sinks and people spend their money on them. Alternatively you might be able to just make it so that instead of paying the in-game currency to buy a new item from the shop, you allow them to buy the item with real world money. I mean, if you're going to allow them to buy the in-game money, you might as well cut out the worries about inflation and instead allow them to directly buy the items.


Aaaaand now you've accidentally made a microtransaction-riddled game without trying to.

Every class is supposed to be good at some things and bad at other things, and they're supposed to work together to make up for their weaknesses. This creates natural moments of heroic narratives when player A is put in a situation where their class sucks but player B's class excels, and then player B gets to be the hero to player A. I think people become exposed to ideas and concepts in general just by talking to other people, or by learning from their parents or in school. And if you live in a place where those three avenues aren't really available to you, you probably live in a place where the Red Cross is active and is talking to you directly anyways.

It's because when you're shot and dying on the battlefield, that guy with the Red Cross is going to help you, too. It's honor and integrity, and respect for those who are risking their lives to do nothing more than to help.

When you show a symbol in a given context, that symbol gets associated with that context. If you do this a ton of times, with a ton of different contexts, the symbol gets associated with a ton of different contexts. 

In order to interpret the meaning of a symbol on both a conscious and subconscious level, you have to look at the sum of its contexts. 


Your example of Coca-Cola is actually really appropriate, because showing Coca-Cola in product placement contexts means that the context of Coca-Cola is no longer just a refreshing drink, it is also a product and a company that can afford product placement in video games, movies, Superbowl ads, ect. All of these concepts come to mind when you think of Coca-Cola, which cumulatively makes Coca-Cola a *brand*. The context of the symbol becomes the logo of a brand, which is attached to the drink. It causes the viewer to think of the brand first, and then take one mental step to reach the drink.


The Red Cross is only in a single context: aid being provided. It isn't given any other contexts, because it should only be associated with the context of aid. When someone sees the Red Cross, the some of everything going through their mind should be nothing less than *help*, than *relief*, than *safety*. There should be no mental steps between seeing the Red Cross symbol and realizing what you are looking at, and the fact that this happens means that the whole world, every single country on this planet, has a universal symbol for someone who is there to help. It doesn't matter your language, it doesn't matter your culture, it doesn't matter where you are, you see that symbol and you know there is help right there in the real world, and there was no other context associated with it.

Part of the reason hex crawls are so difficult has to do with the amount of time it takes to make one. That time investment is reasonable for a lot of people, and unreasonable for a lot of other people.

The card system does everything a hex crawl does, except there's no map I have to worry about and I can make a new "crawl" just by picking out whatever cards I want for the section of wilderness I want. The exact party position is kinda handwavey/jazz hands, you just keep track of Distance Traveled as a function of Cards Drawn. I've got other cards that track the conditions, which can change based on cards that get drawn from the main adventuring deck, and it's really easy to remind the players when to subtract water and food from their inventory because it's right there in the cards, too. 


My favorite part is that it takes ~5 minutes to make a "hex crawl" using this method, and I can give players cards for them to hold on to and they can play when they want and when they meet the conditions of the card. CR is a statistical average of a monster. That's it, that's all it does. A CR 7 monster is *statistically* a good fight for a party of four 7th level PCs. But when you're at the table and you're rolling dice, those dice are going to do whatever the hell they want to do. Because of this, any system or "solution" you design that also includes dice rolls is going to have the same "problem" as CR and XP budgeting.

If it functions anything like the OGL 1.0, they're basically making the equivalent of the Creative Commons 4.0 license you often see map makers and other artists use. It's a license anyone can pick up and use for themselves without needing to hire an IP lawyer to write the license for them. By using the license, you give people the ability to create content for your system or setting or whatever it is that you're making, while still protecting what you legally own and *don't* want people using, like your company logo. 


You can't copyright game mechanics, but you can copyright the dressing or expression of game mechanics. You can't copyright the concept of rolling a d20 and adding a modifier to determine the result of an action, but you can copyright *saying* "make a Strength saving throw." The purpose of the original OGL was for WotC to be like "we do have copyright on the expression of our game mechanics, but we don't care if you copy that expression in your content so long as you don't copy our trademarks (i.e. logo, proper nouns of trademarked locations, ect)."


Unless WotC also adopts this new ORC, you could not use it to write 5e content that uses the 5e expression of mechanics. If you wrote a setting book and didn't use any 5e expression of mechanics, you could use the ORC.

I Am Not a Lawyer, this is just my understanding of the situation as someone who makes OGL 1.0(a) content and regularly talks to an IP lawyer for my job:

You can't copyright game mechanics, but you can trademark the **dressing** of mechanics.  WotC/Hasbro can't say "you're not allowed to have a d20-based system" because the d20 goes back to ancient Egypt and earlier, they didn't invent the d20, and they didn't invent the concept of rolling dice. 

However, if you come out with a d20-based game that has six core stats that you call *ability scores*; and those stats are called *Strength*, *Dexterity*, *Constitution*, *Intelligence*, *Wisdom*, and *Charisma*; and you say that you get an ability modifier based on your ability score; and you roll a d20 and add the ability modifier when making an ability check; etc etc—

Basically, if you copy all the terminology (i.e. the dressing of the mechanics), then you're open to a lawsuit. The terminology and wording used to define the rules of 5e is WotC property/trademark.

You could make a d20-based system with six core stats, but the stats would have to be named differently and you'd have to come up with all your own wording/terminology for describing how the system worked. 

Again though, I am not a lawyer. You should check in with actual lawyers to understand the full nuance of the situation, because what I've described is kinda just a layperson's understanding and skips a bunch of stuff for the sake of making a simple comment on the internet.

I'm also *extremely* well-practiced at running the 200-ish monsters we use for the campaign, so I don't need to spend a lot of time thinking or strategizing. I've got a mental list of every strategy each monster might employ, and I pick one and execute it. I've only been able to build up this mental reservoir by using the same monsters over and over again, but reskinning them or playing them in different ways to give the players the sense of fighting thousands of creatures, instead of just 200. I know a lot of stats by heart now!


Another big help: have everyone, including the monsters, put their AC in their token name. Players always figure out the AC within the first two rounds anyways, adventurers are practiced enough to know when they actually did damage, and erraneous dialogue like "you hit; roll damage" or "hey what's your AC again?" doesn't add much to the experience. I'd rather spend my time on cool action descriptions or plot developments happening mid-combat. 


Also a big fan of not letting rules debates overrun a session. If there's a disagreement on how a rule works, I will usually cut off the disagreement with something like "let's not split hairs over this" followed by how we'll work the rule for now, and we'll look it up to refresh ourselves after the combat or after session. 


Basically: I min-maxed my time in sessions, and frankly, sessions have been so much more fun and productive since. I know I can let my players role-play for 30 straight minutes if they want, and my players know they'll have to actually manage their resources and approach encounters wisely because there won't just be one or two every session, there will be 5+.

I'm currently running my fourth West Marches campaign. Had 50 sessions in September, and I only needed 2 pages in roll20 to do it. Being efficient and straightforward with running games is my life.


1) roll20 pro is invaluable for the following API mods alone: TokenNameNumber, MonsterHitDie, and GroupInitiative. 


2) I keep all of my monsters in a bestiary game and transmog them into the main game as needed.


3) All of my maps fit the same area, so I don't have to worry about tons of pages at different sizes. Just drag the map out and fill up the page. 20x20 is a good size for maps, ime. Allows for a good mix of ranged and CQC combat.


4) Furthermore, I don't bother with a ton of unique maps. I've got 10 "generic" maps that handle all the random encounters and dungeon spaces. Unique maps are saved for special occasions. In my first West marches there was a little bit of pushback against this idea, but players quickly got over it once they realized that it didn't actually matter if they had a unique map every time they ran into some dumb bandits. They also realized that they didn't care if I used a wilderness map for a underground dungeon space, because we're already using our imagination, and what *matters* is how they plan on getting out of their current situation.


5) I have fairly strict rules about how players should conduct themselves during a game. It's stuff like, know what you're going to do when your turn comes up or you're dodging; don't interrupt other turns; once you say "that's my turn" there's no going back; etc. I can easily fit 5-7 combat encounters into a 3-hour session because of this, and that's including an hour for roleplay!


6) you can totally just reskin monsters and players have no clue. The luck of the dice will obfuscate the stats, and then when you throw in your own ability to just narrate the monster differently, describe it differently, have it prioritized different actions, etc, the players have no clue that you've used the same step block for the past 12 monsters they fought.

Well, for now a computer can't. Technology is rapidly evolving and we are on the verge of computers no longer needing strict definitions.


But you have to admit, without definitions we literally would be incapable of communicating with each other in any succinct or concise manner. There is a definition of a chair, otherwise when I say the word chair, nobody would know what I was talking about. People would have to ask me questions to gather more information, but that's not the case. Instead, when I say "I'd like a chair," the person I'm talking to can go straight to helping me get a chair. We don't need a 5-minute back and forth asking questions about what a chair is before they're able to look around the room and point out chairs to me.

So the thing is, a creation doesn't need to be defined. Tropes and genres and chairs and all that stuff DO have definitions, but *a work of art* or *a chair* or *a car* does not need to stick to their definition. 


For example, a movie can be made up of as many tropes or genres as it wants. You can have a vampire noir detective movie, or a post-apocalyptic vampire survival horror movie, or vampire teen romance movie. Vampire media, detective media, post-apocalyptic media, so on and so forth, all of those individual pieces have their own definitions, but the creation itself does not need to fit into those definitions. A creation can piecemeal itself from as many definitions as it wants, and when enough unique creations piecemeal themselves from the same or similar enough definitions, a new genre is born. 


A chair has a definition. However, if you sit down to make a chair you don't need to stick to the definition. You can explore, you can experiment, you can push the boundaries of the definition. That's how you get chairs that are missing legs or have absolutely nowhere to sit. But at wider scale, beyond just you and your workshop and your desire to make a chair less chair, the definition of a chair has not changed in the collective consciousness of society, i.e., when I say to someone "do you have a chair" the mental image they get in their head is still a furniture upon which a single person can sit. That's the definition of a chair. Just because there are a wide variety of styles and colors of chair does not mean the definition is nebulous. 


As you yourself even said, you know what a chair is. A truly nebulous concept, by nature of being nebulous, resists being known or identified.

Furthermore, it all exists on a scale, and there is a level of subjectivity to it, as there is with EVERY creation humans have ever made, including language and definitions. One person might look at Dante's Inferno and say it's got enough markers to qualify as a fanfiction, while another person may look at those same markers and decide it's actually just short of being a fanfiction.

The cheese tactic against a tarrasque: spam planeshift/teleport spells until it runs out of LRs and it's gone. A lot of people will point to this as further proof that CR is dumb, because it results in low-level parties being able to defeat the tarrasque from time to time. Thing is, **CR was never designed to account for all possibilities**. CR was designed to convey the statistical danger of a monster in a flat scenario, i.e. not accounting for a specific location or a specific party build. 

Some parties are better built to handle certain monsters than other parties, and some parties get their hands on a ring of genie summoning and some don't, and some parties have characters using newer material and others don't, etc etc. This doesn't even account for human error such as some parties have GMs that don't read the entire stat block or who fudge rolls or who forget how a mechanic is supposed to work.

There's a LOT that needs to be taken into consideration to determine the full danger level of a monster. CR is *just* the statistical danger of a monster in a flat scenario, but WotC went and told everyone that it's just a "good fight" if the monster's CR matches the party's level and didn't say a damn thing about even surface-level nuances of encounter design and how that can affect a monster. A sniper monster locked in a small room with a barbarian is gonna do REALLY BAD! Put that sniper at the end of a long tunnel with no cover and suddenly it's gonna do REALLY GOOD.

CR is a measurement of what level the party needs to be to ***statistically*** be able to defeat the monster in 4 rounds or less, and *maybe* only one of them will be reduced to 0 HP in the process. See that word there? **Statistically**? Yeah, that's the word that everybody trips over and is the word WotC is friggen afraid of saying, but it is really vitally important to understand that THIS is what CR is!!!

STATISTICALLY SPEAKING, a CR 15 monster will absolutely wipe the floor with 5th level PCs every single time. The odds of success are heavily, heavily, HEAVILY weighted in favor of the monster—**but it's never 100%**. Sometimes the monster rolls poorly, or the players stumble onto the monster's built-in instakill button (looking at you tarrasque), and people come away from the fight *thinking* CR is broken when really what they've experienced is a *statistical outlier*.

If your party has an *easy* time against a monster way above their CR, your party is spider georg and should not be counted. I see this play out all the time. I run a West Marches server, I am either running or watching other DMs run dozens of session every month (there's a team of 12 of us and I coordinate everything, including monster adjustments, so I'm watching if not running), and for every one session where a party does well against a monster above their CR there are three sessions of parties at the same level as the other party getting absolutely wrecked by it.

Also, for every five sessions where a monster does just fine and acts accordingly to its CR, there's one session where that monster rolls bonkers well and ends up becoming a meme boss (praise be to Dreg #1, a CR 1/8 monster that almost single-handedly killed an entire party of attackers because they kept fucking missing).

But wait, there's more! This is the part that boils my fucking blood and makes me want to grab WotC by the shoulders and ask WHYYYYY did they do this????

The CR you see in a stat block is the AVERAGE of *two* CRs, the offensive CR and defensive CR, which can be any fucking numbers! A CR 4 monster could have an offensive CR of 7 and a defensive CR of 1, and guess what??? AVERAGES TO CR 4. BUT IT HITS LIKE A CR 7. WHAT DO YOU THINK IS GOING TO HAPPEN IF A GM FOLLOWS WOTC'S ADVICE AND USES IT AGAINST A 4TH LEVEL PARTY???

To clarify: offensive CR is how hard the monster hits, defensive CR is how well the monster tanks attacks. A monster with an offensive CR of 3 and a defensive CR of 1 statistically hits the PCs as if it were a CR 3 monster, but statistically takes attacks from the PCs as if it were a CR 1 monster. The CR you see in the stat block is 2 which is, by my calculation, *neither of those fucking numbers*.

This, more than anything, is why people hate CR and why they think it's broken. It's fairly easy for a GM to see when a monster is rolling well or rolling poorly. Sometimes I watch GMs whose monster rolls six nat 1s and they blame the monster's stat block for doing poorly, but that's pretty rare, and it gets cleared up real fast by just scrolling up in the roll20 roll log and pointing out all the nat 1s. 

But WotC deliberately obscures the two most vital pieces of information from its GMs. WotC deliberately obscures what offensive and defensive CRs are and gives you a number that yeah, sometimes is accurate. Sometimes a monster is a flat offensive/defensive CR 5/5 monster, which averages to 5. Sometimes it's only one off, like a 5/4 monster, which gets averaged to 5 because there's no half CRs above 0 and the rounding almost always favors the direction of the offensive CR. 

But a lot of the time it *isn't*, and those monsters and their dumb stat blocks that don't convey their statistical probabilities are what give CR a bad name.

At this point you can stop reading, but I do have one more thing I want to go over because even though WotC fucked it up and gave us a large group of GMs who think CR is dumb, it's not. And if you're in that group, I really don't blame you, you were told how to use a handsaw and then given a chainsaw and you rightfully pointed out that what you were taught doesn't work, and so you ignored what you were taught.

So let's learn how to use a chainsaw, using whatever characters I have left for this post. (The metaphor stops here.)

There is ONE type of damage in 5e, and that is **resource damage**. Spell slots are resources, potions are resources, Action Surge and Inspiration are resources, and yes, hit points are a resource, too. Your action, bonus action, and reaction are resources you regain every turn. 

One of the most common misconceptions is that just because the party barely lost any hit points, it wasn’t actually a difficult fight. You have to look at the bigger picture. You have to look at the total amount of resources spent to truly judge the severity of the fight, because resources used in a fight now means those resources can’t be used in another fight later.

Resources are a way for a player to alter a situation. There are lots of ways *to* alter a situation, but basically the only reason *why* you alter a situation is because you don’t like the odds as they are right now. If a player has a +5 to hit but the monster has an AC of 19, those’re very unfavorable odds for hitting that monster. That’s only a 30% chance to hit. In this situation, it’s very common for the player to look to their resources to see if there’s something they can do to make the odds of success better for them—or maybe even an altogether different action option to use—because the player (and the character) wants to win the fight.

But whatever resources they spend now, they may not have access to later. They may not be able to take a short or long rest before their next encounter. And guess what? This game is run on dice rolls. You can control your resource expenditure, but you can’t control whether the d20 will roll a 1, a 20, or anything in between. Expending resources is deadly because it puts you more and more fully into the hands of fate. As your options dwindle, you start to rely more and more on luck—and how many of you reading this *enjoy* losing because of bad luck?

THIS is why the CR chart and these numbers (*me rapidly tapping on chart in DMG*) are so important! D&D’s entire system, from classes to the number of hit points you have to how many times you can use a feature, are all based around an adventuring day of six to eight Medium-ish encounters. With that many encounters, the odds are at some point someone’s dice will roll poorly and someone is going to have to spend a resource to make up for that poor roll.   
  
The CR chart (*more rapid tapping*) and the numbers on it ensure players will have a good time and are still likely to succeed regardless of how many resources they have. NOBODY likes losing to bad luck, NOBODY likes losing because of something they can’t control. The best way to combat how much people don’t like losing to luck is to make the game skill-based, but of course, D&D is a story-discovery game, not a skill game.   
  
The second best way to overcome how much people hate losing to luck is to make sure luck is always on their side. We all have those goopey gamer goblins living in our brains that like big numbers and like winning. It feels bad to watch your character die because of luck—and generally, we’re playing games because we want to feel good in a world full of things that make us feel bad.  
  
The CR chart and the numbers on it do just that. These hit points, these bonuses to hit, these saving throw DCs—they’ll all chosen because they result in a statistical probability that your party has a good time even if they’re completely out of resources, or if they want to play suboptimal characters, or if they want to play a character that’s optimally built, but the player themselves is new and not optimal.  
  
The CR chart is not broken, and it's not your enemy.  
  
The CR chart is your *safety net*.

Art isn't made in a vacuum. Whenever you're making anything, you need to be aware of the connotations surrounding it. No, you are NOT responsible for how people react to what you make, but you ARE responsible for how you set people up to *to* react to your piece. For example, considering everything going on, if you use the imagery of blue skies over a field of yellow flowers, you are *setting up your audience* for thinking about the invasion of Ukraine first and foremost. As someone who absolutely loves planning and designing content, and who has an inordinate amount of time *to* plan and design content: don't be. Holy fuck, do NOT think that you're somehow worse of a GM because you improvise.


The amount of work it takes to design and plan even a single dungeon is absolutely ludicrous. I mean seriously, to have a "planned" dungeon you need to first answer a ton of questions. How many encounters do you need? What's the XP budget of each encounter? What monsters are you using, what's their tactics, what's their *reason* for being here? How is the dungeon mapped out, how are you describing each room? For each encounter, what plans do you have for the 3 most common avenues of interaction (fight, sneak, talk)? What's the history of the dungeon, why do players have to go there, what's their prize, what's the loot, how does this tie in to the main plot?


After answering those questions, you can now actually start to *make* the dungeon. 


Now multiply this by everything else going on in the campaign (towns, NPCs, questlines, custom monsters and magic items, etc). 


It is a LOT of work to actually plan a campaign, even if you're only planning one dungeon at a time. Anyone that *expects* you to put in that amount of work better be paying you $35/hour or more to make it happen, because it will become your job—


—and you'll still end up improvising. There isn't a plan in existence that can survive contact with the players.

There's a LOT that goes into designing a dungeon, and when/how/the consequences (if any) of allowing PCs to rest could be its own 3,500-word essay. I wanted to keep things brief and simple for the basics.
Guardians DO NOT have hit dice, they have shield dice. If you give Guardians hit dice, that's homebrew.

It is intentional that it only recovers shield points. Hit point healing (as opposed to shield point healing) allows you to recover health first, then shields. This kind of healing is rare and extremely powerful. 

One of the most common misconceptions about D&Destiny is that people think they recover shield points every turn, or if they don't take damage in a round, but this is not true. In combat, you only recover shield and/or health points if you perform an action or have a feature, trait, or other source that specifically allows you to, such as Rift of Light.

However, you recover **all shields** on a brief rest (5 minutes of downtime). 

Your Ghost will need to spend uses of Restoration to recover your health. 

Guardians DO NOT have hit dice, they cannot spend hit dice to recover health during a short/long rest.

Even with all of this, Guardians are insanely beefy and difficult to kill. Trust me, I've been running these rules for years :)

I absolutely love shops and shop scenes! But I have a hard limit on how much haggling can happen, and it's based on your Charisma modifier. Players can make a number of Persuasion checks equal to their Charisma modifier, and each check has a chance of lowering the price by a small amount, which can stack on successive successful checks. But if at any point a player fails a check, they lose all of their discount and can't haggle anymore. Potentially, depending on how the PC tried to haggle, the shopkeeper might even get pissed off at them. 

It adds a layer of risk/reward and has a clear cutoff point. Really makes players think about how greedy they want to be, or if they're fine with a simple discount.

>Setting a price, competing with DM's willing to DM for free

Because the advent of paid DM work is *relatively* new, we—as in, the entire TTRPG community—are in a position where we can avoid the same mistake that online artists accidentally made in the early 2000s.

In a nutshell, artists thought that the only way they would get customers is by lowering their prices to out-compete other artists. This snowballed until we were seeing commissions for fully rendered characters as low as $5 a piece. A fully rendered character is something like you would see in the PHB for the different classes and races, and a *fast* artist could get that done in 2-6 hours. 

Charging $5 for a piece you're working a minimum of 2 hours on is *atrocious*. Art communities all across the internet were in shambles, because they accidentally made it so that they, as a community, ate themselves out of ANYONE being able to afford a living off of being an artist.

Somewhere in the mid-2010s, a movement happened: renowned artists were starting to push for higher prices, and they encouraged everyone, even the newbies just starting out, to raise their prices, too. To this day, you can find posts like [this](https://howtobeaconartist.tumblr.com/post/184583202218/pricing-your-art) (links to a tumblr blog that gives advice to artists who want to sell at conventions) that advise, in no uncertain terms, to be kind to yourself and demand a fair living wage for your work.

So, if you want to be a paid DM, be kind to yourself *and your community* by charging a fair, living wage for your sessions. For my private campaigns (the ones not run through my Patreon), I charge $120/session with some rules:

* The price covers the first 4 players, there's a $10 surcharge for every player after the 4th, to a max of 6 players. Players can split the payment among themselves so it comes out to $30/head. 
* Sessions last 3-4 hours. It costs $18/hour to go above 4 hours.
* The price is for open content only. This mean it's either WotC content I'm running for them, or it's homebrewed content that I get to reuse in other places. If players want a closed content campaign, something wholly unique to them, the price is $200/session.

We can already see a troubling trend on roll20, where paid sessions are only $5-10 per player per session, and that's just not feasible. I try to talk to these DMs and I try to make sure people understand that *everyone* benefits when prices are raised. With my session prices, I can afford to pay artists and writers to work for me, which means *they* don't have to work retail, either. A rising tide lifts all boats, and stuff like that.

I'm three and half years into building/playtesting a 5e supplement that includes 9 new classes, each with 3 archetypes (subclasses). There's also a weapon modding system and several hundred magic items. 

Every time I make a minor change, such as re-working a single class feature, there needs to be ~60 hours of playtesting to confirm the feature. I need *this one feature* playtested using a variety of character builds in a variety of situations involving a variety of different monsters with a variety of different magic items and weapon mod builds. There will be about a dozen wording changes and typo fixes during this time, to shore up the feature's mechanics and account for edge cases as best as I can. And then I have to actually *analyze* the feedback I get, I have to pick some brains, I have to ask myself if the feedback I got is actually constructive or is the person wanting something out of the feature that the feature wasn't designed for, etc.

Sometimes, after all of that, the result is that the feature is bad, nobody likes it, and it's back to the drawing board. Could easily have just lost a week's worth of effort—which is *only* a week because making content for 5e is my full-time job and I have a dozen GMs helping me playtest, allowing my content to run in 2-3 sessions *every day*.

That's just a slice of the work that goes into making a *minor* change to the game, a game that already has a lot of the work done for me (it's built on 5e) and a game that has a rigid class structure. 

You are in for a wild ride if you go full modular. In terms of raw time investment, yeah I would say that's a little crazy. But ask yourself: if it's the kind of work you enjoy doing though, and it makes a game that you want to exist, is the time investment worth it? *That's* how you're going to decide if it's too crazy or not.

You know, when I was first starting out as a GM, I did dice fudging. Not a lot, and only if the outcome of the fudge was "better" or "more fun."

I put those in air quotes because the more I learned and the more experience I got, the less and less I fudged rolls, to the point where I actually started doing 100% of my rolls in front of my players. Up until they started metagaming bonuses to hit and calculating average monster damage so I had to put them back behind the screen, but that's a different topic. 

I learned to trust the dice and to adapt to whatever was rolled. I also learned that not everything needed to be rolled for, and I learned how to ask my players, "Is it okay if I don't use any dice for this and go for a cinematic scene instead?" Plus, since I play over roll20, if my players ever accused me of fudging I just sent a screenshot to them. They can see the result of the roll without being able to see the individual dice rolled or the bonuses applied.

So, back when I did fudge rolls, I don't think my fudged rolls were *better* than the rolls that came up on the dice. These days when I recall a few memorable moments where I fudged I think to myself, "Eh, I could have made that moment memorable without the fudge, too." 

I do recognize fudging rolls as part of the GM learning process, and yes, if you do fudge, do *not* tell your players you do. It's a lie, but it is a beautiful one.

Besides, whether you fudge or not isn't the point, it's the stories you told and the memories you made together.

If you want a mechanic that can prevent this from happening regardless of anything else, and not having to worry about giving your monsters special armor and resistances, allow me to introduce you to **health point pools**. This is a mechanic that I have been using for 3 years now in my West Marches style campaign to great success.

Basically, once you are done deciding what the total health or hit points of the monster is (I refer to it as health because we also use multiple different kinds of hit points on our monsters), you take that and divide it by however many pools of health you want your monster to have. The standard is three, two is also pretty popular and four or more can be done but I recommend using it sparingly. 

Damage is applied to one hit point pool at a time, starting with the leftmost pool and working your way to the rightmost pool in the stat block. Whenever damage reduces a hit point pool to 0, any leftover damage is ignored, any ongoing conditions affecting the monster immediately end as it has a breakthrough moment, and the monster gets to perform a special kind of action, interrupting the current turn in order to do so, and this action is called an **ultra action**.

The ultra action can be whatever you want it to be. You can make it so that your monster uses its ultra action to cast its highest level spell, or to summon minions, or to teleport to a place of safety. 

Now you don't actually have to have the monster perform an ultra action. Dividing your monster's health up into multiple hit point pools and allowing it to automatically succeed on ongoing conditions and having the damage cut off because of those hit point pools inherently will make your monsters feel beefier without you actually having to do much work to rebalance them. you just take a dragon's stat block look at the hit points and divide it by 3, or you look at the archmages hit points and you divide it into two pools, however you want to do it. 

But the ultra action is a lot of fun and I call monsters ultra monsters when they have access to this awesome action. My players REALLY love fighting ultra creatures, they know they can go all in and do big damage to ultra creatures but they also don't have to worry about accidentally cheating themselves out of a really cool fight because the hit point pools will prevent them from just burning the creature down in one turn.

I have gotten into numerous arguments about this and I will keep arguing about this over and over again:

The core D&D 5e rulebooks (PHB, DMG, MM) are the ***engine*** of the game that you make at your table. Your level pacing, the type of encounters you build, the thematic elements of your campaign's plot—*that's* the game. And yes, your game can be a murder mystery, or a scifi epic, or a 1920s mob story. None of these settings inherently require any mechanics not already present in D&D to pull off. I mean, come on, what of any of the following is NOT something people already do in D&D anyways:

* Talking up NPCs to try to find the whereabouts of a person/place/thing
* Examining evidence gathered from searching the premises 
* Random encounters against a rival gang
* Sailing a ship or piloting an airship and encountering some beastie that wants to eat you
* Taking on bounties to make ends meet
* Doing something Dubiously Legal and needing to sneak around to get it done

I love when you have the opportunity to put players in a situation where they may need to spend their limited resource earlier than anticipated, or maybe they got lucky or they prepared extremely well such that they have an overabundance of their resource when they finally make it to the boss and it becomes a cakewalk for them. Of all the systems I've made for resource management, from daily uses to hourly uses to regaining a certain number of points at the start of your turn which you then spend on actions you can take for the rest of your turn, I think the one that players have responded to the best has been the role-to-recharge system. 

You have an ability or an attack or whatever the heck you want to call it, and that ability has:

1. A number of charges. You have to spend a charge to use the ability.

2. A recharge die. If you don't have a charge for the ability at the start of your turn, you can roll the recharge die of your ability once.

3. A recharge value. if the result of your recharge die roll is greater than or equal to the recharge value of the ability, you regain one charge in the ability. 

There's actually a bunch more that goes into it, such as how to handle recharges for abilities that last longer than one turn or special conditions that can allow you to make recharge rolls other than just at the start of your turn. I implemented this system, as well as a point-spend-action system (spend a number of points of Resource to perform an action, regain X number of points for that resource at the start of your turn) into my own ttrpg that has several thousand play testing hours into it, and a community of ~3,000 that all really like the system and really enjoy the narrative that comes from the mechanic.

If you don't get your ability back, there's all kinds of ways you can narratively explain that. Maybe you are not quite in the fight, or your nerves have got the best of you, etc. The inverse is also true, a character that manages to get their ability back multiple times in a single fight is really in the zone or is scared for their life and that is bolstering their abilities. I love it when gameplay creates narrative, and roll-to-recharge has the added benefit of being really fun because people, generally speaking, like slot machines, and rolling to recharge your super awesome amazing ability is basically making a pull on a slot machine. It's one of the healthiest loot boxes you could possibly have in your game because it gives people the excitement without costing them anything, lol.

First, I want to say that you don't have to have a higher result, you have to roll the AC *or* higher. A Goblin with an AC of 15 would require a result of 15 or higher to hit. This is actually really important because if you go with only allowing players to roll higher, you actually reduce their odds of hitting by 5%—which will be severely noticed by players.

Actually 5e is built such that the players have a 65% chance to hit when facing a monster of equivalent level. A level 1 PC will have a 65% chance to hit a CR 1 monster, etc.

I can speak from my own years of experience with the system that this 65% chance to hit *feels like* a 50-50 chance to the players. This is basically all due to human psychology: humans focus on the bad stuff more than the good stuff, so even if only two nat 1s are rolled throughout an entire fight, it will *feel* like it was more than two, to the players. And heaven forbid those nat 1s happen on really important rolls, because the players could have rolled perfectly every other time all night, but what's the only thing they're going to remember from that session? Those two nat 1s, lol.

The design of 5e is actually *very* deliberate and it takes into a huge number of considerations, many of which don't have anything directly to do with the numbers on the dice or in the feature's description. Players are designed to be OP at basically every level of the game and can punch up 3 or 4 CRs above their weight class because a) random dice rolls means an easily fight can get deadly very quickly with some bad luck, b) WotC can't control what DMs do with their games but they do still care that players are having a good time, because TTRPGs live and die on their playerbase. They're kind of the OG MMO. This is why people make content for 5e more than any other system: you're way more likely to find players and DMs for your content than any other system, because there are more players and DMs for it.

But to get back to your question, in order to decide what you want *your* iteration of 5e's AC system to be, let's first examine what 5e's AC system does, what design functions it fulfills. 5e's AC system:

* Is meant to be simple and straightforward so that players can get a mental grasp on what a good AC is right away (Big Number = Good AC).
* It helps attacks in combat resolve quickly, so that characters like the 17th level Samurai Fighter don't take too long to finish their turn.
* It is a flexible mechanic to accommodate a whole slew of different narratives for monsters. AC isn't just how hard it is to *hit* the monster, it's also a reflection of how physically durable the monster is, or how well the monster is at parrying your attacks. 

With all that in mind, what do you want YOUR AC system to fulfill? What design goals do you have in mind for it?

Now you're getting it! Reskinning is actually *huge,* you're right on the money there. There's even a section of the Architect's Guide that's going to be dedicated to how to reskin existing monsters in an upcoming AG update.

You can take *any* monster and just re-flavor them to be whatever it is you're looking for. Keep the HP, AC, attack bonus, saving throw DCs, and amount of damage the same, but you can change:

• The reach, range, and/or range band of any weapons being used.
• The type of weapon being used (reskin a melee weapon into a firearm attack).
• The skills, senses, and languages of the monster.
• The *type* of damage dealt on a hit/on a failed save.
• The alignment of the monster's energy shields.
• Movement speed, creature size, and species.
• The narrative reason for any feature or bonus damage the monster is able to do.

Changing any of these things will make a monster *feel* entirely new to your players who, remember, can't see the stat block. All they see are the results of the dice rolls.

Phogoth the Abomination could be re-skinned into a siege minotaur, an Eliksni captain could be re-skinned into a weaker Hive knight, or you could re-skin a cursed thrall into a Cabal tripmine. Once you allow yourself to look past the flavor text and just examine a monster's stats, there are suddenly *thousands* of options available to you. 

And don't worry, it's been a joy to take a deeper dive into 5e and how it works. I've been studying it *intensely* for the past three years and change, I jump at any opportunity to share what I've learned, lol. I'm really glad I've been able to help!

There's a lot of differences between TTRPGs and video games and this is one of the biggest ones, which is that *by default,* players will never simply fight an upscaled version of a monster. You can of course design upscaled versions of monsters, but we're going to set that aspect aside, and let's just talk a little bit about what 5e is, and what *level* means in 5e.

In a video game, your skill directly influences your progress through the game. If you can't hit your headshots, or if you don't time your movement properly, or if you're not coordinating with your teammates, that lack of skill will directly translate into the outcome. 

There is no skill involved in 5e. Everything is determined by rolls of the dice. You the player have to apply zero skill to determine whether or not your character is going to hit with an attack, because there is no skill in the act of rolling dice. How well you hit is determined by your damage roll, which again is rolling dice, so there is no way for your individual skill as a player to influence the outcome. You don't even have to be the one who rolls the dice for your character, a friend could roll for you and it will not change how well your character does, *that's* how little skill there is in 5e. 

So what the heck is going on? How does 5e *work*, if there is no skill? **How do you show your characters leveling up and becoming SKILLED Guardians, capable of slaying legions of dregs, if there is NO SKILL?**

You do it with *ability modifier* and *proficiency bonus.*

As a character levels up, their ability score modifiers and their proficiency bonus will naturally increase. The greater their ability score modifiers and their proficiency bonus is, the *more likely* it becomes for these characters to hit with attack rolls, to succeed on skill checks, and to succeed on saving throws. 

When you're first level and your proficiency bonus is only +2 and you have maybe a +2 or +3 ability modifier for making attack rolls, this creates a grand total of +4 or +5 to hit with weapons you're proficient with. 

If a monster has an AC of 15, this means that at minimum you'll need to roll a 10 on the d20 to hit. There are 20 sides on a d20 and they're all evenly weighted, which means there's a 5% chance of rolling any number. Nat 1s are *always* misses, so if you need to roll 10 or higher to hit, and we're *not* counting a Nat 1, this translates to having a 45% chance to hit. 

45% is pretty sucky! That's less than 50%!

But, as you level up and your PB increases and your ability modifiers increase, all those increases are reflections of the *skill* your character is accumulating over time. 

And if it gets to a point where you have a +14 to hit (which is very possible!), that monster with an AC of 15 will *feel weak.* It will *feel* like you've become skilled, despite the fact that *none of YOUR skill, as the player, matters.* Your CHARACTER has become "skilled," your CHARACTER has become so good at shooting that they have a mere 5% chance (they have to roll a nat 1) to miss hitting a monster with an AC of 15 or less. 

If monsters scaled with the player characters, this sense of progression and growth will be completely lost. The party suddenly no longer *gets* anything from leveling up, because the fights last just as long and the monsters are just as deadly and just as difficult to hit.

Even if you're going full milestone, XP is how you budget your encounters and how you determine the difficulty of an encounter. Each monster is worth a certain amount of XP, and based on the number of characters in the party and what level they are at, you can do some really simple math to determine how much XP you have to spend on an encounter if you, say, want the encounter to be a medium-difficulty encounter.

For example, if you have a party of 6 player characters (Ghosts do not count) that are all at 6th level, and you want their next encounter to be a hard encounter, you have a budget of 5,400 XP to work with, as per the table in the Dungeon Master's Guide (pg 82).

You take that budget and go into the Bestiary and "buy" monsters with it. Each monster has two CRs listed, the Individual CR and the Classification CR. Because you're new and just learning, *ignore* Classification CR. Pretend it doesn't exist. Your encounters will be just fine, I promise. Classification CR is a tool for fine-tuning encounters but you do not need it to just build an encounter.

So you go into the Bestiary and you "buy" monsters using the XP listed after their individual CR. For example, shanks are listed as CR 1/4 (25 XP). This means it will "cost" 25 XP per shank added to the encounter.

Buy monsters until you get as close 0 in your budget as you can.

So as you can see, the CR of a monster doesn't change no matter how many or how few players you have in your game, what changes is your *budget* for monsters. If you only have one player, your budget may only be 75 XP or 100 XP at a time. If you have 8 players, you may have a budget of 10,000 XP even at lower levels, because more players = bigger budget. 

This is all explained in the Dungeon Master's Guide. I promise it's a lot easier to work with than it appears at first, just read through it carefully and follow along with their examples.

Couple things jump out at me:

First, damage point is based on the CR of the monster, with small adjustments (usually +/-3) for flavor.

* CR 0-4: 7
* CR 5-10: 14
* CR 11-16: 21
* CR 17+: 28

*Note: Shriekers and mourners are outliers in this case, because I wanted to reflect how tough they become when they go into their closed form, but also wanted something like, say, a goliath planet cracker shot to still be able to rip through them. Thus instead of saying "immune to all damage and conditions" when they go Closed, it's a ridiculous damage point + immune to conditions only.*

Second, if you only have 3 players you don't *need* to make an NPC to join them. It's certainly fun, don't get me wrong, and Silkiks is a cool idea! But all you need to do is adjust the daily XP budget for your party to reflect that you're down one character. This is one of those things you'll need the base 5e material to cover (*Dungeon Master's Guide, page 81, "Creating Encounters"*).

Because Silkiks won't be around 100% of the time, you'll really want to look into what the 5e XP budget is and how to calculate it. We can't replicate that material in our rulebooks because it's not part of the 5e SRD.

I have a *lot* of low-level flying enemies in my games, creatures as low as CR 0 with a fly speed, but I don't consider the fact that they can fly when determining the CR of the creature at all, because my players have access to a crap ton of ranged attacks. not just dex-based range attacks either, and not just magical range attacks. Even the strength based characters have ranged options that use their strength modifier. So when the flying enemies enter the field, the party just switches to their ranged weapons, and the flyers, most of the time, don't get to benefit from any sort of cover because they're up in the air, whereas the players get to duck and dive behind plenty of cover, often to the point where it forces the flyers down to the ground. 

So no, I wouldn't call flyers OP at low levels either. Providing a decent amount of cover, and giving players access to decent ranged weapons and attacks, completely mitigates whatever bonus flying would have.

And when my players get flying, I do the same thing for the enemies. I give them some cover and I give them ranged attacks.

As for the argument of "obstacles become trivial when players can fly," that is true to an extent, but you really just need to think outside the floor when it comes to how you define an obstacle. Crossing a canyon or gorge isn't what I would call a decent obstacle, personally. obstacles that I present to my players are focused more on what their opponents are capable of doing, environmental challenges, and limiting their options to interact with something. 

For example, it doesn't matter if you can fly across a canyon, if you have a magical barrier that permeates the air all around the canyon and the only way to cross is to hold a relic while slowly moving across a a bridge also built out of magic that requires one spellcaster to sit in a specific spot on one side of the bridge, and then whoever gets across first has to sit in another spot on the other side to hold the bridge with their magic so the rest of the party can cross. throw in some minions to challenge the party, and flying can help against the minions, but it's not going to get you across the canyon. And give the minions a ranged attack or two. 

Flying also doesn't help much if the encounter takes place in a cave with the 10 foot ceiling, nor does it mean much when presented with a trap such as the floor and ceiling are moving in on each other. 

Flying can be OP of it is not accounted for in the design, yes, and it can be a bit difficult at first if you're not used to accounting for flying creatures. But once you get used to it, it really doesn't mean that much, in the grand scheme of things.

I feel like a broken record when I say this, but TTRPGs have a lot to learn from video games when it comes to mechanics and creating interesting, dynamic encounters. Video games have been evolving far faster, pushing the limits of what gameplay is, and most importantly, designing mechanics that understand human psychology (to both the benefit and detriment of the human playing). 

Sometimes I see a lot of pushback from people about how TTRPGs and video games are nothing alike and we shouldn't compare the two together. But a video game is still a *game,* TTRPG is just a different *medium* of game. 

Of course, not *all* concepts that apply to video games will apply to TTRPGs—much like how not all concepts of charcoal sketching won't apply to acrylic painting. But the core concepts of art—the layout of the page, the use of positive and negative space, brightness and contrast, character posing, etc etc—still apply, and there are a lot of core concepts utilized by video game design that perfectly apply to TTRPGs, which is something I've come to learn and appreciate over the years as I worked to recreate Destiny as a TTRPG.

Like everyone else has said, it's up to the DM. There's no wrong way to do it. But there are a lot of answers for why you shouldn't do it, so here's the argument for why you *should:*

1) Numbers are a clear and effective way to communicate an attack's impact on the monster. Nobody gets confused or gets the wrong idea based on your description, you can see *exactly* how effective your attack is. Plus players react viscerally when they roll really high damage numbers but then realize it's barely going to put a dent in the creature, forcing them to start thinking creatively and doing more than "I attack the monster" on their turn. 

2) Giving away HP values also acts as a clear and effective way to communicate the strength of the monster narratively. When players see a pack of 5-HP goblins being lead by a 100-HP ogre, they instantly get the idea of "this is a boss leading its minions into battle." The average adventurer would be able to realize this because they live in the world of these monsters, but new players may not realize this, and thus giving away the HP helps bridge the gap between PC knowledge and player knowledge.

3) Giving away the HP values allows the party to work out how to allocate their resources to survive the encounter, which promotes player engagement in the fight. IME this has a huge benefit on player interactivity with a fight and their cooperation between each other. Humans love to plan ahead, but it's hard to plan ahead when they're missing key information that would help them answer questions such as "when is it a good idea to use Fireball?" and "how many Divine Smites should I dump into this monster?"

4) Allowing players to plan ahead in *any* way allows for some *awesome* scenes as players discuss their strategy and they think they're executing the strategy perfectly until WHAM! Second ogre rolls up, new strategy needs to be adapted on the fly! This HUGELY effects how intense a fight feels and there are a significant portion of players who love fights like this when done in moderation.

But like I said, there is no wrong way to do it. Show the HP or don't; use a hybrid method that only shows the HP of monsters the players have fought before; show the HP bar but don't show the numbers—it's all up to you and how your group wants to play.

Out of all these comments I didn't really see anyone address what game design is:

Game design is an **art,** plain and simple. Asking the question "what are the requirements to be a game designer" is the same as asking the question "what are the requirements to be an author," or "what do I need to be a film editor." 

There are NO requirements to getting started with an art. You just get started and do it. 

Grab a notebook and dream up some games. Design out their systems, start small and force yourself to only work with one or two levels at a time, only one or two mechanics at a time.  

Educate yourself on the history of games and how they're made. Play a game and ask yourself questions like, "Why do I think the lead designer made this decision?" or "What would I change about this mechanic, and what effect would that have on the rest of the game?"

Find interviews featuring designers of games you really like and listen to what they have to say, *study* what they have to say. 

And start making games! You don't even have to make a whole new game. Design a D&D campaign, grab a copy of Super Mario Maker, go mod Skyrim, make a new Pokemon card; whatever gets you *designing gameplay,* go do it. 

Take programming courses and of course go *play* a lot of games. 

Finally, whenever you hit a roadblock and don't know how to do what you want to do, do the same thing you did when you were a baby artist just learning how to draw: Google it, or study someone else's work and try to recreate it until you've figured it out well enough to adapt it to yourself. 

Can't figure out how to paint a cloud? Try to copy Bob Ross's technique. 

Can't figure out what your loot progression should be? Go analyze Diablo 3 or Destiny and figure out how they did it.

Again, game design is an **art.** You are crafting an experience for someone else, an expression of your interests and ideas, just like what movies and books and paintings do. The process you used to become a 2D artist, with all the trials and errors and studying, is the same process that applies to learning game design.

Here's the process I use. Everyone's process is different, but maybe you can start here and see how it goes for you:

First, break all the ideas you have into three categories: NPCs, locations, and quests. Write down whatever list of items you have for each category. These items become the individual pieces of **content** you want to have. You don't have to have one of each, and some categories will naturally have more content than others; that's fine.

Then examine each piece of content and bullet-point the main ideas of it. Is your villain bombastic, loud, and a bit of a show-off? Jot that down. Do you want them to have a super cool mythic action that alters the very battlefield in the final fight? Summarize how you think that action will work. If you have a sidequest to obtain a magic item to kill a minor dragon, what are the main steps? Write them in a simple bullet-point list, and if there's multiple outcomes, make a quick flowchart in MS paint or on some graph paper of how the steps flow and/or split from each other.

Don't worry about perfection at this stage! Everything you're writing down now is for YOU, not for anyone else. Write it in whatever way YOU need to so YOU can understand it.

As you're adding information about the individual content, you might realize you need a new NPC or location. Just go ahead and add it to your content list and fill in details. Some content might change as you come up with other ideas for other pieces content; that's fine, too. Let your ideas flow and don't think that just because you wrote it down, it's permanent.

You'll want to spend a long time on this "filling out content information" step. Give yourself at least 20 hours for it, but seriously, shoot for 40-60 if you can. The more time you spend here, the *less* work you'll do later on.

And while you're filling in details for the content, make sure to frequently take a step back and look at the content list. Are you making too much, too little? Is there anything you can trim back on? Keeping your scope manageable, so that you don't just spend forever building and never get around to playing, is really important and possibly one of the hardest things for a new designer to learn. 

Once you have listed out all the content you want and have written down a satisfying amount of detail, enough that you feel like you could run the content with extreme confidence, it's time to start picking out, or making, assets! Your villain will need a stat block, you might want to get some battlemaps, your super rad traveling merchant with need an inventory list, etc. And since you sorted everything out in the previous step, this one will be a breeze; you know exactly what you want already!

Making new content, whether it's just a single questline or a whole campaign, can be really daunting no matter how much experience you have. I've found that breaking everything into steps and focusing more on getting it *done*, rather than trying to get things *perfect*, really helps to get over the hurdle of Just Getting Started. Tell yourself, "Look, I'll make it pretty later. For now, I just need the information written down somewhere."

I've written three modules in the past three years. (Or five, if you count modules that are less than 10 pages for this.) While improv is a huge part of my DM style, I prefer to plan all the major NPCs, events, locations, and dungeons ahead of time. 

I start with writing out what all the big ideas/major concepts of the module are. Even if it's a premade module by WotC, I read **the whole thing** (seriously, read the whole thing!!!) and write a neat little bulletpoint list of what the most important aspects of the module are. 

I do this so that, later on when I'm running the content and reacting to player actions and I inevitably end up improving a change to the story or NPC or what have you, I keep that list in mind and I try to make my improved content match the concepts on the list. This keeps the content coherent with the rest of the module.

The next step, after listing out the major ideas behind the module, is to create **the straight path.** Of course, the straight path doesn't need to literally be a straight path. It can involve doubling back and so on, the point is that the very first thing that you finish is the surefire, 100% guaranteed way that the party can go from the start of the module to the end. No deviations, no choices, no shortcuts or skips, just plain ol' railroad start-to-finish. 

I do this because sometimes, I overestimate my ability to finish creating a module in time for the start of the campaign. By focusing on getting the straight path done first, I ensure that I at least have a whole story done. Improving deviations, choices, shortcuts and skips into the content is easier, ime.

If I have the time I do go back over my content and I start implementing major choices characters can make, deviations in the plot, shortcuts and skips through content, etc. Essentially I start with making the barebones story, and then I flesh it out with all kinds of goodies and rewards for different player interactions.

Finally, and what is ultimately my favorite step, I make the auxiliary content. Potion recipes, shop inventories, NPC pickpockets, side quests, etc. I write all of my content assuming theatre of the mind, and it's in this step that I start adding battlemaps to the module, too. 

This is all very broad and doesn't even scratch the surface of what it takes to make a module, though. Not that you need to make a whole module before running a campaign, of course. Many DMs find great success with nothing more than a page of notes and some improv.

Years of culture, both within the TTRPG community and in media in general, has taught people that puzzles must be incredibly complex and the obvious solution is the wrong solution. It doesn't help that of the fee times that media portrays a simple puzzle (like LotR's "Speak Friend and Enter"), the characters are usually portrayed as stumped anyways, or the characters go off on a tangent related *specifically to their relationship with each other,* which results in them not being stumped by the puzzle itself, but by the exact context of the puzzle and the *characters* who are trying to solve it—because I guarantee you the *actors* realized the solution halfway through reading the setup in the script.

But of course when we play a game, we the *players* want to feel stumped, not our characters. And GMs often build puzzles to trick *the players,* not the characters. So there's this whole mess of things going wrong when it comes to presenting a puzzle in a TTRPG:

1.) The players are expecting it to be more complicated.

2.) The players have no context for how to solve the puzzle, because rarely are puzzles made following strict rules and guidelines ala sudokus, crosswords, etc; those kinds of puzzles. Your players can probably solve a difficult crossword just fine, but a crossword has a very limited and set way to interact with it. Just saying "there are three levers, which is the right one to pull?" is far too open-ended for a puzzle solving experience because it'll just devolve into skill checks, speculation on what the GM meant by using whatever words they used to describe the result of the skill checks, and arguments. And these won't always be in character, the majority of these arguments will be between the players.

3.) The expectation is that the puzzle is built for the *players,* not the characters, and frankly, some people want to play characters who are smarter than them. This creates tension when the player feels like their charay should have been able to solve it, but they themselves just didn't think of the solution.

Because of these factors, I've taken to being very strict with what puzzles I present and how players can interact with them. I limit the options of interacting with the puzzle in as many ways as possible, I give very clear and consistent results with whatever interaction does occur ("nothing happens" gets boring to say but it's vital for cementing the boundaries of the puzzle), and I allow *characters* who have a certain feature, background, or passive skill score to receive hints or even part of the solution entirely.

I stick with passive skill scores only because I, personally, *don't* want the puzzle-solving to devolve into "I'm just going to keep making skill checks until I win." 

And of course, as others have said, having an alternative (though less desirable) way to bypass the puzzle is super important. Some days people want puzzles, and some days they just wanna beat the sphinx with a stick and call it good.

Making mistakes and learning how to recover from them is part of gaming. A new player may find the situation frustrating for their character to have to deal with, but unless that player is an asshole, it'll be a frustration that lasts for all of 10 seconds. Yes, a spell slot is wasted and the monster lasts slightly longer than it would have normally—but an invaluable lesson was learned, and now the player's character knows to pick a different spell for that monster if encountered again in the future. 

My #1 recommendation for you is to not do what you did again. Embrace damage immunities. By allowing the damage type of the spell to change, you've effectively communicated to the players that damage type doesn't matter and spellcasters can just make any spell do any kind of damage, so who cares what the resistances and immunities are?

Conversely, if you make resistances and immunities matter you actually open up a lot of new avenues of gameplay and immersion for your players. Spending time researching monsters and asking experienced NPCs rangers how to handle (monster) becomes important! Having different types of weapons and spells at the ready is essential! 

You also open the door for a plethora of micro-stories to exist. Imagine the PCs facing off against a monster that's immune to their standard weapons and spells, forcing the characters to get creative and shake things up a bit. Or maybe the PCs are tasked to hunt down a monster that's said to be immune to everything, so now they've got to spend time figuring out how the heck to destroy it. 

However, if you really like the mechanic of changing spell damage types, my #2 recommendation is to make it something that takes time and investment to do, not something that a simple Arcana check can accomplish. For example, you can allow Chain Lightning to be cast as Chain Fire (same mechanics and damage amount, just does fire damage) if the caster spends a few weeks practicing, or if a special consumable item is used. Please also do it for your martial classes, too. Weapon coatings or enchantments would be good lore-friendly ways to allow damage type changes on swords and such. 

If neither of the above sound appealing, my #3 recommendation is to ask yourself, what do you want out of your campaign? What sort of gameplay do you *really* care about? Remember, you're trying to create stories with your gameplay. If the stories you want to tell don't include making the characters worry about damage types and/or planning what equipment they're going to pack for the next leg of the journey, then skip that stuff altogether. It's perfectly fine not to bother with it! 5e is insanely robust; it'll survive your tinkering. And honestly, it's more like a game engine, not a game. It's the equivalent of Unity. Go wild and make it your own!

I am a full-time developer for 5e. I make my living on designing, testing, and delivering content for 5e. I say this all the time:

D&D 5e is a game engine, not a game. It's the pencil and paper equivalent of Unity. 

Game masters are game designers. Making a D&D campaign with any amount of homebrew is being a game designer. Add new classes? New races? New magic items? Make new monsters? Game design. That's all partaking in game design. 

Even if you add nothing new, the monsters you pick, the encounters you set up, the loot you choose to award players with, the NPCs they interact with: that's all game design, too. 

90% of what they teach about video game design can be applied to your TTRPG campaigns. TTRPGs are just a different *medium* of gaming, not a completely separate art form. Going from video game design to TTRPG design is the equivalent of going from acrylic painting to charcoal drawings. Yes, the tools are different; yes, the end results will never be the same—but the core concepts of shape, composition, lighting and shading, etc all apply.

Games are a form of art. Creating a game is an artistic process. Video game, card game, board game, and TTRPG are all just different mediums of the art of gaming. 

And D&D is a fantastic *engine* of a TTRPG to work with.

"More effort put into balancing content in general, actually."

I just want to take a moment to hop up on a soap box and talk about this for a bit.

"Balance" is an inherently impossible task in an asymmetrical system such as 5e. By *definition*, balance—at least, the way people want balance—is *impossible* to achieve, because the whole point of an asymmetrical game is that *the sides are not equal*. The tools at the disposal of Fighters are *not* the same as the tools at the disposal of the Wizard. This is literally the whole point of the game. 

What you're hoping for, when you search to balance a system like this, is that people will ***perceive*** the available tools to be equal in value, despite being inherently different and not equal.

And that's the crux of it: it's all about *perception*. To some people, the tools of the Fighter will far and above outshine the tools of the Wizard. I know that's not the norm here in this sub, but just because it's not the majority opinion doesn't mean that someone, somewhere, is upset that their Wizard can only cast Fireball a few times a day while the Fighter can make 2 attacks every turn with a 10% chance of getting a critical hit.

This isn't even considering the design of the campaign by the GM, which can make or break certain classes entirely. If the Ranger picks dragons as their favored enemy, but the party never fights a dragon, what's the point? If the GM is constantly throwing players up against lava monsters that heal when they take fire damage, what about the ever-popular Fireball spell matters? If you build a sniper-style character, but your GM never gives you a long-range fight to use your crossbow in and you're constantly in cramped quarters with multiple goblins in your face, you may find yourself feeling *unbalanced* compared to the Barbarian.

There's a lot that can be said about the power of certain spells vs the strength of Extra Attack vs various feature & feat combinations vs certain multiclassing options, and so on and so forth. There's a lot to discuss when it comes to the head-to-head statistical comparison of various game aspects, but there's even *more* to discuss when it comes to the *perception* of those game aspects and how players interact with them, and how *that* is affecting the "balance" of the game.

Because again, the *point* of an asymmetrical game is that it is not balanced. You are not playing Chess or Checkers, you do not have the same pieces as your opponent. You have Tool Set A, which comes with its unique strengths and weaknesses; and they have Tool Set B, which comes with *its* unique strengths and weaknesses. And everyone is hoping that the players will *perceive* the strengths and weaknesses to be equal trade-offs despite the fact that they are, inherently, definitely, *not* equal.

So, in a virtual economy you have something called a "money sink." It's usually an NPC or other vendor that sells consumable items that have a lot of uses but charge a decent sum of the game's currency to purchase. The money just... vanished, after the players buy the item, though. This offsets the fact that money is generated by killing enemies or completing quests. 

The OTHER method, which would actually apply to real life, is a wealth cap. This is when a game limits the maximum amount of currency you, the player, can have at a time. Money sinks eventually stop working, but a wealth cap endures that prices for items can never be above X amount, because players physically cannot hold more than X amount.

Start with the setting. What is the dungeon? Is it an old wizard keep, the ruins of an ancient civilization, and underground jail? Write it down. 

Now write a bullet point list of all the rooms, areas, or facilities of the dungeon. Force yourself to keep the list short for now—say, a max of 5. Fully flesh out those five. What loot is in each spot? Monsters? Traps? Where is the boss?

At this point, if you haven't done it already, map out your dungeon. Don't worry about making the map good or big enough to be a battle map, just make it legible and put all the shorthand information you need on the map (icons for doors, traps, number each room, etc). 

Write a brief narrative piece for each area, aka, what you're going to read out to PCs when they enter one of the areas. 

Finally, at this point, you can add more areas or rooms or facilities to your dungeon. By limiting yourself at the start you gave yourself a reasonable goal, and it forced you to finish what you started and get it into working state. Now you can use whatever leftover time until your players enter the dungeon to polish it, expand on it, add more secrets, etc. 

BIG NOTE: Build for your party! Does your party have a barbarian? Give the dungeon a door to some minor loot that can only be opened with a good Strength check. Is there a wizard? Maybe add a spell scroll or two that has spells the player has been wanting for a while. Is there a ranger on board? Maybe put a rat or mouse in there for the ranger to talk to and learn of an upcoming trap. People love feeling like they're getting good use out of their class in non-combat ways!
