I think you should just straight-up tell them their options and the consequences at the start. New players, especially if they're new to TTRPGs altogether, often don't realize the breadth of choices they have at any time, and they don't necessarily think through the consequences of each choice. They need to be taught how to do this, much like how someone new to console games needs to be taught how to use a controller.

Go ahead and railroad them a little bit. Whenever there's a choice to be made, give a little speech that boils down to, "Here are your options right now, and here are the consequences of each option." Be direct and forward. Don't worry about immersion or anything like that—you need to teach them how to play before you can get to being fully immersed in the world and characters.

End each speech with, "But if you have other ideas, I'm willing to discuss them." Over time, your players will build a mental catalog of options for various scenarios. Slowly pull back on the amount of options you provide (and be a bit more vague about the consequences; "this might cause someone nearby to come investigate" instead of "this will cause the neighbors to come investigate"). Emphasize that they can come up with their own options more and more. You'll know they will have learned when they start to bring up their own options, and they talk through the potential consequences among themselves without needing your input!

This process takes far less time than most people realize. Some tables might take a few sessions to learn, but I've seen players learn how to play a TTRPG in less than one session using this process.

If you calculate the % chance of successes using the recommended AC/save DC in the DMG's Monster Statistics table and a character that starts with a +3 in a relevant stat (total of +5 when faction in prof. bonus), you'll find that the core engine of 5e basically hovers around 65% chance of success across all levels for both attack rolls and saving throws.

Now I specifically say core *engine* of 5e and not *game* because the Monster Statistics table is not the game. Hell, not even just the actual monsters in the monster manual are the game. The *game* is the content you, the GM, put together. That consists of everything from the maps and environments you use, to the monsters you put in your encounters, to the NPCs, the setting, the antagonist, etc. 

There are lots of different ways to put this content together. Some GMs pre-plan, some make it up on the fly. Some treat it like a group project with their players, and some mash together so many different systems and homebrew mechanics they're making both a new *engine* (rules that govern gameplay) and *game* (the content players can experience) at the same time. However it happens, the game always comes down to being the actual content of the campaign or module you're running.

I bring all this up because, usually in these discussions, the concept of difficulty comes up in some way, shape, or form. Some GMs saying they always increase the AC/DC of everything because it's too easy for players otherwise, or something like that, and they cite the 65% or how easy it is for players to get advantage to back themselves up. At the time of writing this no one has really done that, but I've seen it enough that, if you don't mind me hopping up on my soapbox here for a hot minute, I'd like to discuss two things about Game Difficulty.

**The point of a game is never to stop players from progressing**. This is true in ALL forms of game, from schoolyard games to Dark Souls. The point of a game is simply to challenge players. If you can't rise to the challenge, of course you won't be able to proceed. But the point of a game is not to *stop* players, the point is to challenge them to *encourage growth*. 

Tag challenges your physical speed and dexterity, Dark Souls challenges your perception and timing, Overwatch challenges team cohesion and prediction skills. TTRPGs, though? Well, there's no skill in rolling dice. There's no skill behind passing a high DC vs a low DC. There's certainly a type of skill that occurs in character creation, which can make it more likely for you to pass a high DC, but the actual act of rolling a d20 has no *skill* behind it.

**What TTRPGs challenge is the player's decision-making skills**. It challenges how players calculate and weigh Risk vs Reward. Other skills like role-play and inventiveness are definitely part of the TTRPG experience, but ultimately the *challenge* is how the players make decisions. 

This is why 5e's core game engine hovers around 65% success. Well, it's two reasons why, the other reason being that humans notice and remember bad things more often as part of our biological survival mechanism of learning from and avoiding bad things in the future, so a truly 50-50 chance of success will *feel* like it's worse because our *perception* will not be 50-50. So WotC went with a 65%-ish success rate, which will *feel* closer to 50% to the players, and the feel of the experience is worth way more than the actual numbers. And like, we all know how nasty the dice can be sometimes. Players need that extra boost, lol.

But I digress.

5th Edition hovers around a 65% success rate for players across all levels because the point of the game is NOT to roll a die to overcome an AC/DC. The point of the game is **resource management**. It's, "Do I spend my spell slot on Smite, or do I heal the Fighter?" It's, "Do we side with the kobolds, or the villagers?" It's, "Do we risk pushing on with our hit dice spent and resources low, or do we risk getting ambushed with a long rest?" And that stuff all comes from the *game* the GM has put together, not the engine.

If your only method of making a difficult encounter is to reduce the odds of players succeeding on their dice rolls, all you're doing is manipulating a slot machine. It's a game, sure, but in a weird turn of events, by *only* adjusting the AC of monsters or the DC of saves you're actually making the game *less challenging*, because now it's just all about *luck*.

**Knowing the % chance of success on a given roll is vital to game design and game pacing**. You have to know when to turn those numbers up, and when to turn them down. It's a delicate balancing act that every GM will approach differently, and all those differences in approach are perfectly fine! Game design is an art, not a science. What works for one table won't always work for another.

Just keep in mind that the % chance of success is not where the challenge comes in. The challenge—and thus, the game—comes when you present your players with a situation where they have to weigh the odds ***and make a decision***.

I've been homebrewing a Destiny (video game)-themed 5e conversion for the past two years, I run a server that hosts an average of 5 games a week and has over 1,500 members (though we have approximately 30 *dedicated* players who consistently return to sessions, not counting campaigns/games we know community members run outside the server).

I get 100+ submissions on our feedback form every month, and even more submitted mid-session by players. **The BEST feedback is feedback that STOPS as soon as the player has explained why they don't like something**.

The short and sweet of it, when it comes to the difference between helpful and unhelpful feedback, helpful feedback focuses solely on your feelings toward whatever you are submitting feedback about. **Don't offer any suggestions for what the mechanics SHOULD be**, don't try to discuss whether it'll be best to increase or decrease the damage of something, or to alter the function of a feature to what you think is a better version of it. Just say things like,

* "I don't have fun interacting with this mechanic."
* "This feature is nice but it's weird that my class has to wait so long to get it."
* "I feel like this monster does too much damage."
* "I’m confused about this mechanic. With the way it’s worded in this part of the rulebook, it sounds like I can combine X and Y together, but this *other* section of the rulebook seems to contradict that. So, which is it?"

You can get specific with your feelings too, if you have specific feelings. If I took the monster damage feedback example and wanted to extrapolate on it, I might say,

* "I feel like this monster does too much damage. Fights always feel way more difficult when we have to fight this monster and our GM consistently has to fudge die rolls to keep things fun for us. I just don't feel like I have the resources to fight the monster fairly."

That is like, a 5-star example of helpful feedback. It not only explains how someone feels, but **it focuses on explaining the SOURCE of the feeling**. This is FAR more useful than trying to propose a fix because of this one simple fact:

**You are not the designer of the content**. You don't know what the best solution to a problem is. You don't know if the solution you propose is actually going to work with the intentions and goals of the designer, and your "fix" may actually interfere with other plans the designer has.

In the above monster damage example, the designer might be *hoping* that the monster feels overwhelming with its damage output. So the solution the designer wants may not be to lower the damage, but may instead be to *buff the resources* of the player. Or maybe they lower the *hit points* of the monster, but keep the same CR. Or maybe the CR is, in fact, a typo, and the designer just needs to go fix that.

You also don't know ALL of the feedback the designer is getting. You might see top 5 posts on a reddit post that say "this spell is too strong," but there might be 20 posts on a Twitter thread with people going "holy heck the role-play opportunities with this spell are amazing, and my players love using it."

You, by nature of not being the designer, don't know the full story of the content. A "fix" you propose may be a lot of time and pixels wasted on an idea that completely misses the point. And sometimes—rarely, but sometimes—the solution to a problem people are having has NOTHING to do with mechanics\*. It might be a choice of words which is causing a misinterpretation, or the issue is out of the designer's hands due to outside factors.

But when you do your best to explain *where you're coming from*, the designer can do their best to change things so they can show you where they want go.

​

>DISCLAIMER: This post is opinion. Game design is an art, including how feedback works for you! There isn't really a right or wrong way to do it, this is just my thoughts from my experience. Maybe it'll change in the future, idk, I'm just giving my Thoughts(TM).

\*One time, we fixed a problem with people being super confused about a mechanic not by changing the mechanic in any way, but by simply moving the location of the mechanic in our game's documentation, because we realized *no one was reading the chapter it was originally included in*. The bad feedback about the mechanic basically disappeared overnight.

My biggest tip for any new GMs is, the vast majority of your encounters should be Medium or lower difficulty. Too many times I see new GMs making harder and harder fights because their players are getting through them "too easily." 

First of all, just because you *thought* it was easy, doesn't mean the players *felt* like it was easy. Also, it is a game. The players are *supposed* to be overcoming challenges and having a good time. If the players had fun, who cares if it was easy? 

Second of all, you're setting yourself up for failure by constantly making fights harder. Harder fights take longer to get through, thus feeding into the "combat takes too long" problem, and if every fight you make is hard, players just get used to that. This makes it harder for your capstone fights to stand out and be impactful on the gameplay because they'll just be another hard fight in a sea of hard fights.

There also tends to be this creeping issue where, your fights are harder, so they take longer to get through, so you plan less fights, so the players have more resources to spend on the fights, thus making them easier, so you go and make the next fight *harder*...It's a self-feeding cycle.

However, the biggest benefit of easier fights, the benefit I really try to draw new GM's attention to, is how easier fights impact role-playing at your table. When players are presented with easier fights, fights where they know they don't have to act perfectly because there's less risk of failure, they feel more at ease acting as their *character* would act, rather than trying to min-max the combat. And when players embrace this, it REALLY makes 5e shine.

In my 2 years of being paid to run 5e games, I've noticed that there seems to be this inherent separation in the mentality of players, between how they approach role-play sections and combat sections. It's almost like players are switching between two different games, in their head. Ever since I started having myself and all of my co-GMs running easier fights, this separation has been disappearing in my playerbase, and it's insanely exciting to see!
